topic: floor malting barley: steeping to full water, turning the piece and curing on a small kiln

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: cyfrowy tester wilgotnosci ziarna

base: I am floor malting my own barley and the piece is growing very unevenly.
The small kiln at the end of the loft was built for half a quarter at a time.
A digital grain tester on the shelf reads the moisture of every sample I draw.
I steeped this batch for two days with one air rest in the middle.
Was that steep too short, or am I turning the piece too seldom on the floor?
The steep is the likelier fault, since two days rarely brings barley to full water.
Grain that goes to the floor dry in the middle will always chit unevenly.
Aim for about forty five percent moisture before you cast the piece at all.
Two air rests suit most barley, and cold water needs longer than water off the roof.
I steeped the next lot for three days with two air rests as you advised.
The grain tester read forty four percent when I cast the piece on the floor.
The chitting came on evenly this time, right across the whole bed of grain.
How deep should the piece lie, and how often does it want turning now?
Keep the piece four inches deep at first and turn it twice in each day.
As the rootlets lengthen the bed heats itself, so thin it down and turn more often.
A piece left thick will felt together and tear when you finally move it.
Judge the growth by the acrospire, which should reach three quarters up the corn.
The acrospire has reached about three quarters and the corn now rubs to a sweet flour.
The grain tester shows the piece drying slowly on the floor, down to forty percent.
The small kiln is loaded and the fire has been laid since yesterday evening.
Should I start the kiln hot to stop the growth, or come up gently instead?
Come up gently, because heat on wet malt fixes the moisture inside the corn.
Hold the kiln near fifty degrees until the malt is dry to the hand.
Only then raise the fire for the curing, which sets the colour and the flavour.
Turn the malt on the kiln floor every few hours so it dries right through.
I held it at fifty for a day and a night before raising the fire.
The malt came off pale gold and bites crisply between the teeth.
A handful from the far corner, though, still tastes faintly raw and doughy.
Is that corner worth saving, or should the whole floor go back on the kiln?
Do not rekiln the lot, since dried malt loses flavour every time it goes back.
Screen out that corner and spread it thin on the kiln for a few hours.
A raw taste in one corner usually means the air came up unevenly beneath the floor.
Check the tiles there for soot, which blocks the draught more than anything else.
The tiles in that corner were half blocked with soot from the winter before.
I cleared them and the next kilning came off even from one wall to the other.
The malt has been sacked for a month and smells sweet whenever I open it.
How long will it keep, and does it want any particular sort of store?
Sacked malt keeps a year easily, provided the store stays dry and reasonably cool.
Damp is the only real enemy, because malt draws water out of the air readily.
Stand the sacks on pallets and leave a hand's width clear of every wall.
Let it rest a full month before brewing, since fresh malt works badly in the mash.
